hybrid.answer:
**Out of the box: it depends on the leather.** His advice comes from his Blundstone videos, so it's specific to leather boots like those.

- **Most Blundstones:** He reads Blundstone's own FAQ saying most are pretreated, so *Blundstone* (not him) advises against treating them out of the box [1]. He adds his own reasoning: if you treat them again, the product will just roll off [1].
- **Rustic Brown, Crazy Horse or Rustic Black (distressed) leathers:** The FAQ says these don't carry the same pretreatment [2]. Here he strongly recommends treating them [3], warning that if you keep them dry, they'll probably break down sooner [4].
- **His view changed:** In his 2019 review, a puddle test made him take back his claim that the distressed pair wasn't treated [5]. A week later he corrected that after reading the FAQ [6].

Treating will darken the leather [7]. If you hate that, he suggests at least looking into silicone 'nano' sprays, which change the look less but also need reapplying [8].

**How often: his latest answer (2022) is "when they need it."** He admits he doesn't know an exact schedule and personally treats them when he feels they need it [9]. His cues:
- **Looks or feels dry:** add more oils [10].
- **Not beading water:** add more wax [10].
- **Dirty:** clean them regularly, because dirt wears the leather down faster [10].

In 2019 he was more specific:
- You may have to wax them every month, maybe every week if you're super hard on them [11].
- If you haven't conditioned leather in a few months, do it [12].

**How he does it:** clean, then condition, then wax [13]. Go with thin coats, since he says less is more at first [14].

- If they look or feel dry, they need oil or conditioner.
- If water isn't beading on top, they need more wax [12].
- Clean them regularly when they're dirty, because dirt wears leather down faster [13].

The order is always clean, condition, wax [14]. As a rough benchmark from 2019, he said anything leather you haven't conditioned in a few months should get conditioned [15].

In his first Blundstone review (2019) he was more cautious. He said you *may* have to wax them every month, or maybe every week if you're really hard on them [16]. He has since moved to the "when they need it" approach.

questions.question: So if I buy the levis 501 shrink to fit will they get tighter after washing?

hybrid.answer:
**Yes, in his experience they shrink and get tighter once they get wet, mostly in the waist.** That's why he recommends sizing up.

**Sizing (his most recent advice):** In 2025 he says you put the 501 STF in the bathtub and it shrinks, so "You should usually go two sizes up" [1]. In his 2021 review he said Levi's advice is to go two sizes bigger in the waist and two inches longer, and that it took him four pairs of 501s to admit Levi's is right [2]. If you follow that, he says the jeans will fit normally after you get them wet [3].

**How hot you wash them matters:** In his 2023 comparison he says a shrunk STF would be a lot smaller from the start if you threw it in the dryer [4]. His advice is not to put STFs in the dryer or rinse them in very hot water, and you can get a really nice fit [5].

**What happened with his own pair:**
- In 2019 he didn't follow Levi's advice. After a hot soak and sun drying, the waist was very tight ("definitely around the waist"), but the length looked pretty much the same [6][7].
- A week later the waist and upper thigh had stretched enough that he could wear a belt [8].
- After a year he said that 29 waist was barely wearable at first but is now a really good fit. He would have gone longer in the length, though [9].

So expect them to get tighter after the first soak or wash, especially at the waist, and then loosen somewhat as you wear them.

hybrid.answer:
**His rule of thumb: size up about two in the waist and go longer in the length.** Applied to your usual 33x30, that would point to roughly a 35 waist and a 32 length. That's just his general rule applied to your numbers, though. He never compares 501 STF sizing to the 502 or any other Levi's fit, so he hasn't said how your 502 size carries over.

**His most recent advice (2025):** For the 501 STF he says it won't simply shrink to fit, and that "You should usually go two sizes up" [1].

**Why he sizes up (2023):** He normally wears a size 30, and he bought his STFs two sizes up, in a 32 [2]. He measured them and found the waist isn't vanity sized, which is why you go up two: they shrink down [3]. After shrinking, his pair still came out smaller than a regular rinsed 501 [4].

**Length (2021):** He passes on Levi's own advice of two sizes bigger in the waist and two inches longer than you'd normally wear [5]. He admits he ignored it, and it took him four pairs of 501s to accept that Levi's is right [6].

**Where he went wrong (2019):** In his first STF video he deliberately didn't follow Levi's sizing, because jeans are usually too long on him [7]. After the soak the waist was extremely tight [8]. The length, on the other hand, barely seemed to shrink at all [9]. So his own experience is clearest on the waist; on length he went from skipping the extra length to recommending it.

**One related tip:** Your final size also depends on how you shrink them. He says not to rinse them in very hot water or put them in the dryer if you want a really nice fit [10].

questions.question: Why do you cuff your jeans?

hybrid.answer:
He's speaking about his own reasons across three videos. Mostly he cuffs **to control length and to make wider jeans fit his style**, though for a while he preferred wearing jeans down over his boots.

**Most recent (2020 one-year 501 update):** He says he would have bought a 32 length, but he cuffs the 501s anyway, because he doesn't think his current style suits uncuffed, wider-legged pants [1].

**Late 2019 (L.L.Bean boots review):** He says he always used to cuff his jeans, but now likes them down over his boots a bit more [2]. He thinks that look calms the Bean boots down as a loud fashion statement [2]. For that style he suggests a 7 to 7.5 inch leg opening pulled down over the boot [3].

**Mid 2019 (original 501 STF video):** He explains that for him "it's all about length." If jeans look too long, he thinks they just look bad, and that matters most to him [4]. He also says the cuff shouldn't be too thick [4]. A basic cuff made the wide, unshrunk 501s fit and feel a little better [4]. A pin roll slimmed them a bit more, though they were still wider than he likes [5].

questions.question: So do you prefer [the Red Wing 3335s] over the 1907s?

hybrid.answer:
**Not as clearly as he used to.** His most recent take (September 2023) is hedged. He notes he's "on record" calling the 3335s his favourite Red Wings, says they "still might be but… probably not," and adds that the 875s, 1907s and Iron Rangers each have characteristics he really likes [1]. He still values the 3335s for being stitch-down, lighter and more nimble, which suits walking or a light hike [1]. Even so, they were on his sell list in that collection cull [2].

**His earlier view (October 2022) was a firm yes.** He called the 3335s his favourite boots he'd ever owned and said they beat the 1907s, the 875s and his Blundstones [3]. His reasons:
- **How he uses boots:** he goes on hikes and walks in the woods rather than doing heritage work, so he found them "a dramatically better all-around boot" [3].
- **Looks:** he thinks they "look way cooler" [4].
- **Sole:** he likes the 3335's dense Vibram mini lug sole, which he doesn't expect to break down as fast as the crepe soles on the 1907s and 875s [5].

**Where the 1907 wins, even in that review:** he said the 1907s and 875s are more beefily built, so if you need a tough boot, the 3335s are probably not the ones to get [3]. He also didn't think the 3335's stitch-down construction gives it much edge over the Goodyear-welted 1907s. Part of his reasoning is that the 3335 uses only a single stitch, so it isn't "some infinitely better level than 1907s or 875s" in that regard [6].

questions.question: How does the made in England boot stack up to Solovairs? [Dr. Martens]

hybrid.answer:
**In his only head-to-head take (April 2022), he recommends Solovair over Made in England Dr. Martens.** He calls Solovair the cheaper, better-built option, unless the yellow stitching matters to you.

**Why he prefers Solovair**
- **Price vs. what you get:** He thinks most of the Made in England premium (about a third of the boot price) pays for the "made in England" part itself [1]. For pure value and a better-built boot, he points to Solovair [2], which he says is actually cheaper [3].
- **Leather and midsoles are roughly even:** He credits Made in England Docs with better leather that will age fine, and better midsoles, but considers both probably on par with Solovair [4][5].
- **Shank and comfort:** Solovair boots have a shank, so he finds them more comfortable over long periods [6]. Docs are easier to break in at first, while Solovairs are tougher to break in but give more comfort down the line [7].
- **Resoling:** He says Solovairs are Goodyear welted in a more conventional way, so they're easier to resole [8].
- **Same look and heritage:** He describes Solovair as one of the original makers of Dr. Martens [6], and says their derby eight-eye is essentially the same boot [9].

**When Made in England wins:** Solovair doesn't do the yellow stitching. If that's a big deal to you, he says you have to get the Made in England Docs [10].

**A caveat on his own pair:** After eight wears, his Solovairs had a ripped back tab and a snapped lace. He believes it was a manufacturing defect and had contacted them [11]. He also notes the video wasn't sponsored by either company [12].

**Later view (May 2023):** His newer video compares Made in England 1460s with the cheaper Made in Thailand pair and doesn't mention Solovair. He still concludes the Made in England boots probably aren't objectively worth the extra $90 [13] and are really for mega fans of the brand [14]. That fits his earlier reluctance to pay the Made in England premium, but he hasn't revisited the Solovair comparison since 2022.

questions.question: Is vintage Patagonia better than new Patagonia?

hybrid.answer:
**In his head-to-heads (Oct 2025), vintage Patagonia wins both rounds: decisively on sweaters, and only reluctantly on fleece.**

**Sweaters: a clear win for vintage.** He calls the comparison of the modern 50th Anniversary Rugby Sweater with a vintage Patagonia sweater "not a fair comparison" [1]. The vintage one is 100% virgin worsted wool [2]. He gives the point to vintage "by a mile" [2] and tells fans to get one on eBay as fast as they can [3]. He allows that sweaters were once real climbing tools, so they had to be built differently [2]. He also says the modern rugby sweater uses mechanically recycled wool, which is weaker than virgin wool, blended with nylon to keep its strength [4].

**Fleece: a hedged point for vintage.** He compared a 1988 made-in-USA Retro-X with the modern version. He calls the vintage one "a freaking tank": stiffer, heavier, denser and with higher pile [5]. But his warmth test found the new one didn't lose any warmth [5]. Apart from the fabric, the modern one differs mainly in a laminated, more water-resistant pocket and the lack of a wind-stopping placket [6]. He doubts these changes were cost-cutting, since polyester is cheap and fleece is shaved to height anyway. He thinks they were more likely made for comfort or ease of wear [6][7]. In the end he says, "I guess vintage Patagonia should get one point," while joking that Patagonia might send him rub-test data showing the new stuff is better [8].

**Better Sweater complaints.** Some people say the modern Better Sweater pills more and doesn't last as long. That's their claim, and he says it "doesn't make any sense to me" [9]. Recycled synthetics can be as strong as virgin fibre if chemically recycled, or weaker if mechanically recycled. Patagonia seems to do both, but he doesn't know which is used where [10].

**In fairness to new Patagonia,** he notes that synthetic fabric technology is improving faster than any other in textiles [10]. He also says Patagonia has very high testing standards [8].

He doesn't give a single overall verdict beyond these two points.

questions.question: Is it my impression or RL has MUCH lower quality now than what it used to?

hybrid.answer:
If by "RL" you mean Ralph Lauren, he doesn't cover it in these videos, so there's no take from him on whether Ralph Lauren's quality has dropped.

He has looked at the same "they don't make them like they used to" question for other brands:

- **The general pattern (2025 Patagonia video):** He argues that when brands went global, many "beacons of quality" from the 70s to 90s realized they could make more for less, and that all they needed to do was "cut quality to make things faster" [1]. He names L.L.Bean and Levi's in that context, not Ralph Lauren [2]. In his view, Patagonia stood out by keeping a 70s-style business model with strong warranties, repairs and quality control [3].
- **Levi's specifically (2023):** His verdict was that Levi's aren't made like they used to be [4]. Still, he found the gap in quality and durability between modern and vintage 501s "is not as much as you probably would think." Much of what he loves about vintage pairs makes them cooler rather than better jeans [5].

So he does think some big brands cut quality as they scaled, but he hasn't looked at Ralph Lauren.

full.answer:
**He hasn't covered Gucci jeans.** None of The Iron Snail's videos review or mention Gucci denim, so there's no verdict from him on whether they're worth the money.

He has talked about what drives denim prices and where he finds value, which may help:

- **His value pick:** In his 2025 value ranking, he says non-selvedge denim is faster and cheaper to make, so "you can get similar or even better quality for a much lower price" [1]. He gives Wrangler's rigid Cowboy Cut the number one spot for value [2].
- **Why some jeans cost more:** For Japanese selvedge, he points to slow, half-width shuttle looms. He says that makes the denim "around four times more expensive" than regular denim [3].
- **Exclusivity as a price driver:** Reviewing Levi's $260 LVC jeans, he cites a Naked & Famous comment arguing that what you're mainly paying for is exclusivity [4]. That's their claim, not a finding of his. His own theory is that Levi's "could price these genes lower" [5].

None of this is about Gucci specifically, though.
